## 1. Environment & Architecture

For this workflow, we leverage specialized packages to handle unstructured archival data, extract specific clinical entities, and perform unsupervised machine learning on text corpuses.

```{r packages, results='hide'}
# Define required dependencies
req_pkgs <- c("tidyverse", "tidytext", "tesseract", "magick", 
              "udpipe", "igraph", "ggraph", "textrank", 
              "topicmodels", "pdftools")

# Install missing packages
missing <- req_pkgs[!(req_pkgs %in% installed.packages()[,"Package"])]
if(length(missing)) install.packages(missing)

# Load all libraries
invisible(lapply(req_pkgs, library, character.only = TRUE))

```

---

## 2. Archival Data: Image Preprocessing for OCR

Raw OCR often fails on historical medical records due to noise or skew. We use `magick` to mathematically clean the image *before* feeding it to `tesseract`.

```{r image_preprocessing}
# 1. Generate a "noisy, skewed" mock archival document
raw_scan <- image_blank(width = 600, height = 250, color = "gray90") %>%
  image_annotate("CLINICAL NOTE - 1984\nPt presents with acute myocardial infarction.\nAdministered IV nitroglycerin.\nPrognosis: Guarded.", 
                 size = 22, color = "black", gravity = "center") %>%
  image_rotate(3.5) %>% # Simulate a bad scanner feed
  image_noise("gaussian") # Simulate archival degradation

# 2. Preprocess (Deskew, Grayscale, Contrast Enhancement)
cleaned_scan <- raw_scan %>%
  image_deskew(threshold = 40) %>%
  image_convert(type = "grayscale") %>%
  image_contrast(sharpen = 1) %>%
  image_enhance()

# 3. Extract text
eng_engine <- tesseract("eng")
extracted_text <- tesseract::ocr(cleaned_scan, engine = eng_engine)

cat("--- OCR OUTPUT ---\n")
cat(extracted_text)

```

---

## 3. Comparative Corpus Analysis (TF-IDF)

To find terms that distinguish different medical guidelines, we use **Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF)**, which penalizes words common across all documents and rewards uniquely defining terminology.

```{r tf_idf}
# Mock corpus of medical guidelines
guidelines <- tibble(
  specialty = c(rep("Cardiology", 3), rep("Neurology", 3), rep("Oncology", 3)),
  text = c(
    "Hypertension is a primary driver of cardiovascular disease.",
    "Heart failure patients require diligent blood pressure monitoring.",
    "Acute myocardial infarction requires rapid catheterization.",
    
    "Ischemic stroke is a major neurological emergency.",
    "Patients with acute stroke require rapid neurological assessment.",
    "Migraine management involves identifying triggers and neuroimaging.",
    
    "Chemotherapy protocols depend heavily on initial tumor staging.",
    "Radiation therapy may be used in conjunction with surgical resection.",
    "Tumor biomarkers increasingly guide targeted oncology treatments."
  )
)

# Tokenize and calculate TF-IDF
guidelines %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  count(specialty, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  bind_tf_idf(word, specialty, n) %>%
  group_by(specialty) %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 4) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(word = reorder(word, tf_idf)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(tf_idf, word, fill = specialty)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~specialty, ncol = 3, scales = "free") +
  labs(title = "Highest TF-IDF Words by Medical Specialty") +
  theme_minimal()

```

---

## 4. Entity Extraction (Regular Expressions)

In clinical text, you often need to extract precise data points—dosages, blood pressure readings, or ages—buried within paragraphs. We use **Regular Expressions (Regex)** via `stringr` for pattern matching.

```{r regex_extraction}
# Mock messy clinical notes
clinical_notes <- tibble(
  patient_id = c("P-001", "P-002", "P-003"),
  note = c("Patient is a 54yo male. Prescribed Amoxicillin 500mg PO BID.",
           "42yo female patient. Refill Lisinopril 10mg daily. BP 130/85.",
           "Pt is a 71yo male. Administered 1000mg Acetaminophen. BP 145/90.")
)

# Extract structured data using RegEx patterns
structured_data <- clinical_notes %>%
  mutate(
    age = str_extract(note, "\\d{2}(?=yo)"),           # Digits followed by 'yo'
    dosage = str_extract(note, "\\d{1,4}mg"),          # 1-4 digits followed by 'mg'
    blood_pressure = str_extract(note, "\\d{2,3}/\\d{2,3}") # Digits/Digits
  )

# Display the neatly extracted data
knitr::kable(structured_data)

```

---

## 5. Topic Modeling (LDA)

When handed 10,000 documents without labels, researchers use **Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA)** to mathematically discover the hidden "topics" pervading the corpus. LDA assumes every document is a mixture of topics, and every topic is a mixture of words.

```{r lda_topic_modeling}
# 1. Convert our tidy data into a Document-Term Matrix (DTM)
dtm <- guidelines %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  count(specialty, word) %>%
  cast_dtm(document = specialty, term = word, value = n)

# 2. Run the LDA model (asking it to find 2 underlying topics)
lda_model <- LDA(dtm, k = 2, control = list(seed = 1234))

# 3. Extract the per-topic-per-word probabilities (Beta)
topic_probabilities <- tidy(lda_model, matrix = "beta")

# 4. Visualize the top terms defining each mathematically discovered topic
topic_probabilities %>%
  group_by(topic) %>%
  slice_max(beta, n = 5) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(topic, -beta) %>%
  mutate(term = reorder_within(term, beta, topic)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(beta, term, fill = factor(topic))) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ topic, scales = "free") +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  labs(title = "Top Terms Defining Unsupervised Topics",
       subtitle = "Topic 1 aligns with Oncology; Topic 2 aligns with Cardio/Neuro",
       x = "Beta (Probability word belongs to topic)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

```

---

## 6. Semantic Networks (N-grams)

To understand context, we extract **bigrams** (two-word phrases) and visualize how medical concepts map together using network graphs.

```{r bigram_networks}
bigram_counts <- guidelines %>%
  unnest_tokens(bigram, text, token = "ngrams", n = 2) %>%
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ") %>%
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words$word, !word2 \%in\% stop_words$word) %>%
  count(word1, word2, sort = TRUE)

# Plot network using ggraph
set.seed(42)
bigram_counts %>%
  filter(n > 0) %>%
  graph_from_data_frame() %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(edge_alpha = n), arrow = a(length = unit(3, 'mm')), end_cap = circle(2, 'mm')) +
  geom_node_point(color = "darkred", size = 4) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), vjust = 1.5, size = 4) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Semantic Network of Medical Guidelines")

```

---

## 7. Advanced NLP: Lemmatization & Keyword Extraction (RAKE)

Standard tidy approaches strip away grammar. For deep qualitative analysis, `udpipe` performs **Part-of-Speech tagging** and **Lemmatization**. We use this to execute Rapid Automatic Keyword Extraction (RAKE) to find complex, multi-word medical concepts based on grammar rules.

```{r advanced_nlp, results='hide'}
# Load the English language model
ud_model <- udpipe_download_model(language = "english")
ud_english <- udpipe_load_model(ud_model$file_model)

# Annotate our entire corpus
annotations <- udpipe_annotate(ud_english, x = guidelines$text, doc_id = guidelines$specialty)
nlp_data <- as.data.frame(annotations)

```

```{r rake_extraction}
# Execute RAKE hunting for adjacent Nouns and Adjectives
rake_stats <- keywords_rake(x = nlp_data, 
                            term = "lemma", 
                            group = "doc_id", 
                            relevant = nlp_data$upos %in% c("NOUN", "ADJ"),
                            n_min = 2)

# Display top extracted concepts
rake_stats %>%
  arrange(desc(rake)) %>%
  select(keyword, freq, rake) %>%
  head(5) %>%
  knitr::kable()

```

## 8. Scaling Up: Ingesting Real PDFs

While this demo uses mock dataframes, researchers usually start with folders full of PDFs. The `pdftools` package bridges this gap seamlessly.

```{r pdf_ingestion_example, eval=FALSE}
# NOTE: This chunk is set to eval=FALSE so it doesn't fail during compilation.
# In a real workflow, point this to a folder of actual PDF guidelines.

pdf_directory <- "path/to/your/pdf/folder"
pdf_files <- list.files(pdf_directory, pattern = "\\.pdf$", full.names = TRUE)

# Read all PDFs into a single dataframe
corpus_df <- tibble(file_path = pdf_files) %>%
  mutate(
    # Extract text from the PDF
    raw_text = map(file_path, pdftools::pdf_text),
    # Paste pages together into a single string per document
    clean_text = map_chr(raw_text, ~ paste(.x, collapse = " ")) 
  )

# You can now pass `corpus_df` directly into the tidytext pipelines above!

```
